detail:
Mayo Clinic describes treatment choices for trigeminal neuralgia as depending on the cause of the pain, medical history, side effects, risks, and how quickly and how long a treatment relieves pain. Medicines are often recommended first, and sometimes no other treatment is needed. The medicine classes Mayo Clinic lists include antiseizure medicines as the most common choice, along with antispasmodic agents and botulinum toxin injections in some cases; when the pain is caused by another condition, such as multiple sclerosis, that underlying condition may also need treatment.

When medicines do not work and the pain is caused by a blood vessel pressing on the trigeminal nerve, Mayo Clinic describes microvascular decompression, a surgery that moves the vessel away from the nerve, as often providing the most durable relief, while noting that it may come with serious risks. Other options in the source include brain stereotactic radiosurgery, a noninvasive focused radiation procedure, and rhizotomy, a minimally invasive procedure that treats the nerve to block pain signals.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing trigeminal neuralgia and its treatments.
summary: Mayo Clinic describes trigeminal neuralgia treatment that usually starts with antiseizure medicines, with microvascular decompression described as often providing the most durable relief when a blood vessel presses on the nerve, plus radiosurgery and rhizotomy options.
takeaways: medicines are usually the first line of treatment, per the source
Mayo Clinic describes microvascular decompression as often the most durable relief
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
title: Trigeminal Neuralgia: from first-line medicines to surgical options
